en.title: Why A Ben Solo Star Wars Film Was Never Truly Needed
en.summary: Reports surfaced last year of a potential Steven Soderbergh-directed Star Wars film focusing on Ben Solo. Despite fan campaigns, the project never materialized, and Adam Driver has definitively closed the door on further Star Wars appearances.
en.body:
The Star Wars galaxy is vast, filled with stories both told and yet to be explored. Last year, a fascinating 'what if' emerged: **Lucasfilm** reportedly turned down **"The Hunt for Ben Solo"**, a project that would have seen **Adam Driver** reprise his role as the complex character following his redemption in **"Star Wars: Episode IX – The Rise of Skywalker."** The film was slated to be directed by the acclaimed **Steven Soderbergh**, with **Scott Z. Burns** penning the script. This news ignited a passionate response from a segment of the fanbase, eager to see more of Ben Solo's journey.

Fan fervor reached a fever pitch, with organized campaigns including banner planes flying over the **Disney** lot and electronic billboards in Times Square. Even **Rian Johnson**, director of **"Star Wars: Episode VIII – The Last Jedi,"** lent his support. However, despite the considerable enthusiasm, the dream of a Soderbergh-directed Ben Solo film seems to have definitively ended. **Adam Driver** himself has stated on multiple occasions, including the *Smartless* podcast and *The Rich Eisen Show*, that he is "not doing any more" Star Wars, emphatically concluding, "it's over. No more Star Wars."

## Moving Forward, Not Backwards

While the prospect of a **Steven Soderbergh** Star Wars film is undeniably exciting, and the idea of further exploring Ben Solo's post-redemption arc holds appeal, it's perhaps a good thing that **"The Hunt for Ben Solo"** never came to fruition. The very existence of such a project, had it been greenlit, could have been interpreted as an attempt to course-correct the narrative direction of the sequel trilogy. **"The Rise of Skywalker"** itself was seen by some as a reaction to perceived fan dissatisfaction with **"The Last Jedi."** Introducing a new film focused on Ben Solo so soon after his ultimate fate in Episode IX might have risked undermining the conclusion of his arc and the broader thematic resolutions of the trilogy.

## The Unfolding Galaxy

The Star Wars saga has always been about evolution and looking towards the future. From the original trilogy's hopeful ending to the expansion into numerous Disney+ series and upcoming films like **"The Mandalorian and Grogu,"** the franchise thrives on introducing new characters and challenges. While Ben Solo's journey was a compelling part of the sequel era, dwelling too long on his past might detract from the potential for fresh narratives. The sequel trilogy, for all its divisive moments, did introduce significant new elements to the galaxy, and continuing to build upon those foundations, rather than revisiting a recently concluded storyline, feels like the more dynamic path forward for **Star Wars**.

## What's Next

With **Adam Driver** seemingly finished with the galaxy far, far away, the focus for **Star Wars** is now firmly on new stories and characters. Future projects will continue to expand the universe in unexpected directions.

content_raw: Last year, Star Wars fans were shocked by the revelation that Lucasfilm turned down The Hunt for Ben Solo , a story that would have followed The Artist Formerly Known as Kylo Ren as he dealt with his redemption in the wake of Star Wars: Episode IX – The Rise of Skywalker . Not only would Adam Driver have reprised his role as Ben Solo, but none other than Steven Soderbergh was tapped to direct, with Scott Z. Burns ( World War Z ) penning the script. Ultimately, the project never went through as then-Disney heads Bob Iger and Alan Bergman spent a lengthy amount of time reading the script, and Driver and Soderbergh deciding to move on. “I’m not doing any more,” Driver told the Smartless podcast in 2024 . Yet that didn’t stop fans from campaigning to get Lucasfilm to reverse their decision. A plane flew a banner over the Disney lot. Fans paid to have an electronic billboard in Times Square. Even Rian Johnson, who turned out in of the best modern Star Wars projects in the form of Star Wars: Episode VIII – The Last Jedi , threw his support behind the Solo film. However, while the idea of a Steven Soderbergh-directed Star Wars film is a promising prospect, it’s a good thing that The Hunt for Ben Solo never came to pass. (And now it almost certainly never will, with Driver recently telling The Rich Eisen Show “Yeah, it’s over. No more Star Wars.) For one thing, it would have felt like an attempt to course correct the franchise after The Rise of Skywalker , which itself was an attempt to try and course correct on the (utterly wrong) assumption that The Last Jedi broke the franchise. For all its ups and downs, the Star Wars sequel trilogy did bring some major changes to the galaxy far, far away, and it’s better to move forward rather than look backwards. Some fans might point out that The Hunt for Ben Solo would give the former Kylo Ren more character development. Those fans are forgetting that such a story exists in a miniseries published by Marvel Comics: The Rise of Kylo Ren , The Reign of Kylo Ren , and The Fall of Kylo Ren by Charles Soule, Will Sliney, and Luke Ross. In this trilogy, readers witness Ben Solo’s descent into darkness and his inner war with himself as he rules the First Order. It’s truly a well-written character piece that adds far more depth to the Sequel Trilogy and Ben himself. Some of the best Star Wars stories aren’t on the big screen, and these comics are proof of that. Another major factor that must be considered is how the campaign to bring The Hunt for Ben Solo to life ran parallel to the “Release the Snyder Cut” movement that plagued the internet for years. While the latter campaign did feel fulfilled by the release of Zack Snyder’s Justice League , a large part of the reason why it was greenlit is that HBO Max needed a big draw as it then was only a year old and in need of some angry nerds’ subscription dollars.
